newsitem.title: CHINA: Rival Koreas sign aid agreement for hungry North.
newsitem.headline: Rival Koreas sign aid agreement for hungry North.

text.p: South Korea on Monday agreed to send thousands of tonnes of food aid to the famine-threatened North under the first direct agreement between the Red Cross societies of the Cold War rivals in more than a decade.

Seoul officials hailed the agreement to ship 50,000 tonnes of food aid to the North by the end of July as a symbolic lifting of the veil of isolation and ignorance hung around the North's hungry people.

"We have no doubt that this agreement will (help build momentum) to increase mutual cooperation between (the) two Koreas on the basis of humanitarianism," said South Korean Red Cross official Kogh Young-kee.
The accord was the first between the Red Cross societies of the rivals since a 1985 pact on hometown visits by displaced families, Kogh told reporters after the signing ceremony in a Beijing hotel.

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean civil war ended in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even basic food aid a delicate diplomatic affair.

North Korea, which takes self-reliance as its guiding ideology, has sought to limit any direct contact involved in taking grain from the South, while Seoul wants to maximise exchanges and make sure its aid is clearly labelled.

Pyongyang had now agreed that some aid would be labelled as coming from the South -- a move that would ease suspicions and help Northeners see the economic success of their neighbours, said Chang Moon-ik, spokesman of Seoul's Beijing embassy.
"Then North Korean people...may be awakened," Chang said.
The agreement would also allow Southern donors to specify the areas and even the individuals they wanted to benefit from the food they sent, he said.
"If we deliver to designated areas and certain persons, then this influence will spread in North Korea in the future," he said. "It will also help to promote the inter-Korea dialogue."

Corn would account for most of the 50,000 tonnes of food promised by Seoul as the first stage of direct Red Cross assistance, but wheat, milk powder and instant noodles would also be donated, South Korean officials said.

Under the accord, which was reached after three days of often difficult talks in Beijing, the aid would be transported through two ports in North Korea and also by land across the isolated nation's border with China.
Seoul officials said they were disappointed that Pyongyang had not accepted shipments through the town of Panmunjom, which straddles the militarised border between the two Koreas.
"We are very disappointed not to send through Panmunjom...because most of our people want to use the Panmunjom area," said one official after the signing ceremony.
Seoul had argued that the Panmunjom route was the most direct and cost-effective and that shipping through China meant extra delays getting the food to hungry Northern compatriots.
Inter-Korean talks in Beijing earlier this month failed after South Korea declined to say how much aid it would supply. Seoul later promised to ship food worth $8 million.

Seoul officials said agreement in the latest round of Beijing talks was delayed by Pyongyang's demands for a larger food package as well as by differences over how to transport, package and distribute it.

While Monday's pledge of 50,000 tonnes of food is dwarfed by aid promised by other donors -- the European Commission said last Friday it was sending 155,000 tonnes -- it is expected to lead to further shipments from the prosperous South.
